[PAPER_0035, relevance_score=0.449] Methods and Procedures

Two similar experiments were conducted and will be jointly described below. Experiment 2 was identical to Experiment 1 except it added a syllable counting orienting task during study and collected decision confidence during N3AFC test trials. Subjects were recruited through Prolific.co and the experiments were scripted in jspsych (De Leeuw, 2015) and hosted on pavlovia.org.

[PAPER_0036, relevance_score=0.462] Subjects

For Experiment 1, 98 subjects were recruited through the prolific.co research participant pool and 88 completed the study. These individuals were paid $6.56/hr of participation. For Experiment 2, 94 subjects were recruited through prolific.co and 85 completed the study. They were paid $8.01/hr reflecting the increased minimum wage for the site during the later experiment. Subjects were tested in accordance with Washington University's IRB procedures and screened on prolific for English as a first language and for being aged between 18 and 35.

[PAPER_0037, relevance_score=0.443] Target sample size was 84 which yields 80% power for a correlation of .30. Recruitment slots were opened on Prolific for 90 to 95 subjects in anticipation of modest attrition and additional increments of approximately five were added until the target size was exceeded. In both experiments the data were analyzed at Ns of approximately five subjects to ensure that the program was collecting the required variables for analysis.

[PAPER_0048, relevance_score=0.282] Transparency and Openness

The raw data and main analysis and simulation scripts for both experiments are available at the Open Science Foundation at https://osf.io/hg7nc (Dobbins, 2021). Experiment 1 was also pre-registered there (https://osf.io/j3wqb). The current paper departs from the pre-registration in two ways. First, it used a more restrictive cut off for parameter outliers, adopting the more conventional 2.5 versus 3 standard deviation cut off.

[PAPER_0049, relevance_score=0.264] This resulted in discarding one subject in Experiment 1 based on the uvsd parameters. This subject yielded a negative d' indicating a failed fit. The second departure was a new analysis whereby the uvsd model was applied to wholly synthetic old/new and N3AFC data generated from the dpsd model.

This analysis was developed during the analysis of Experiment 1 data to attempt to explain why the uvsd model empirically failed in the manner it did.

[PAPER_0038, relevance_score=0.264] Materials and Procedure

Stimulus words were randomly sampled for each participant from a 1,216-item pool, with an average of 7.09 letters and 2.34 syllables and a Kucera-Francis frequency of 8.85. Each participant underwent four study/test cycles of interleaved old/new and N3AFC recognition, beginning with old/new recognition. In each cycle the test was preceded by intentional study of 60 words.

[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.445] Model Fitting and Statistical Analysis

Each subject's old/new recognition test data were collapsed across the two tests yielding 120 target and lure trials. These data were fit via maximum likelihood using the ROC Toolbox for Matlab (Koen et al., 2017) providing fits for both the uvsd and dpsd models. Fit statistics are available at https://osf.io/hg7nc but are a minor focus of the current study.

[PAPER_0052, relevance_score=0.359] Fit Data

In the Discussion I explain why fit statistics are not useful for assessing the construct validity of non-nested decision models. Nonetheless, for completeness a corrected and uncorrected fit index for the uvsd and dpsd models was compared. For Experiment 1, the Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Ms. = 607.97 vs. 607.59; t[87] = 1.47, p = .144) did not reliably differ across the dpsd and uvsd models respectively.

[PAPER_0060, relevance_score=0.336] Turing to the multiple regression analyses, Tables 7 to 9 demonstrate that the uvsd d' parameter positively and uniquely predicts N3AFC accuracy (Experiments 1 and 2) and N3AFC confidence (Experiment 2), as it should under the model. However, the behavior of the sigma parameter is again unanticipated by the uvsd model. In all three cases the standardized coefficients linking sigma to behavior are markedly shrunken compared to the analogous pairwise correlations in Tables 5 & 6.

[PAPER_0096, relevance_score=0.354] Only the dpsd model parameters were predictive. Moreover, when this full model was compared to a model restricted to the dpsd parameters, there was no reliable difference (F[2,169] = .25, p = .781) indicating that the uvsd parameters within the full model yielded no reliable increase in incremental validity.
